usage: 건네주다 (= 건네다 + 주다) is the polite everyday way to ask someone to pass an object to a third person; the bare 건네세요 alone sounds oddly clinical.
A frequent collocation — 돈을/봉투를/명함을 건네다, always for placing a physical thing directly into someone's hand.
to strike up / address a few words
A fixed idiom: 말을 건네다 means to break the ice and speak to someone, not to literally pass words; learn it as a set phrase.
Pairs naturally with gestures of greeting; shows 건네다 can extend something social, not only a held object.
examples: 물 좀 건네줘
Pass me the water
Casual 반말 between friends; 건네줘 = 건네 + 줘 drops politeness for someone close.
친구에게 책을 건넸어요
I handed the book to my friend
The particle 에게 marks the person who receives — this is the core sentence frame for 건네다.
선생님이 책을 받더니 조용히 메모를 건넸어요
The teacher took the book and then quietly handed over a note
Real-situation, slightly formal narration; note 건네다 fits a composed, deliberate hand-over.
nuance: 건네다 is the verb for the deliberate, hand-to-hand act of passing a physical object to a person who is right next to you — money, a card, a cup. Compare it with 주다 (to give): 주다 only says ownership transfers and can happen at any distance, while 건네다 foregrounds the physical gesture of the hand reaching across the gap, so a server '건네준다' a menu but a company '준다' a bonus. In real speech it usually appears as 건네주다 (건네 + 주다) when you do it as a favor: 이거 건네주세요. Note the special idiom 말을 건네다 'to strike up a conversation', which English speakers wrongly read literally as 'hand over words'. Conjugation is easy because the stem ends in the vowel ㅔ: 건네 + 어 contracts to plain 건네, so the 요-form is 건네요 (never 건네어요) and the past is 건넸어요 (never 건네었어요).

Don't reach for 건네다 when something is mailed or sent across a distance — that is 보내다; 건네다 needs the receiver to be within arm's reach.
Don't translate 'hand over words' literally; 말을 건네다 is an idiom for addressing/greeting someone, so use it whole rather than building it word by word.

usage: Please give back the book you borrowed
The default verb for returning anything borrowed; 빌린 + noun + 돌려주다 is the textbook pattern.
to put / give back the way it was
Beyond objects, 돌려주다 covers restoring a state, e.g. undoing a change.
to win someone's heart back / change their mind
A figurative use — returning someone's affection or persuading them to come around.
Common at a register; here 돌려주다 returns money that was over-handed.
examples: 우산 내일 돌려줄게
I'll give the umbrella back tomorrow
반말 promise; -ㄹ게 commits the speaker to a future action for the listener's benefit.
이거 누구한테 돌려줘야 해요?
Who do I have to give this back to?
Casual 한테 marks the person who should receive it back — the everyday spoken counterpart of 에게.
보증금은 퇴실하실 때 전액 돌려드립니다
The deposit is returned in full when you check out
Real-situation honorific: to a customer you upgrade 돌려주다 → 돌려드리다 to raise the listener.
nuance: 돌려주다 is the compound 돌리다 (to turn / send back) + 주다 (to give), so it literally means 'turn it back and give it' — the standard word for returning a borrowed thing, money, or even a changed situation to its rightful place. Contrast it sharply with 갚다, which is narrower and means to settle a debt or repay an obligation (빚을 갚다, 은혜를 갚다); you 돌려주다 a borrowed umbrella but you 갚다 a loan, because 갚다 carries the sense of clearing what you owe, not just physically handing an item back. When the receiver outranks you, swap 주다 for the humble 드리다 → 돌려드리다 (보증금을 돌려드립니다). Because the verb ends in 주다, every form follows 주다 exactly: 줘 → 돌려줘, 줬어요 → 돌려줬어요, 주세요 → 돌려주세요 — there are no irregular surprises.

Don't split it as 돌려 주다 thinking 주다 is a separate helper here — 돌려주다 is a settled single verb meaning 'give back', so keep it together.

english: to look after / pack for someone
usage: A warm parting line; 챙겨 먹다 means to look after your own meals, a hugely common caring phrase.
챙기다's core sense is gathering what's needed; +주다 means you do that gathering for another person.
to make a fuss of someone's birthday
Idiomatic — to remember and celebrate someone's special day, showing 챙기다 covers caring about events, not just objects.
Set wish-phrase; here 챙기다 means to look after / not neglect something important.
examples: 엄마가 도시락을 챙겨줬어
Mom packed a lunchbox for me
반말 narration; the classic image of 챙겨주다 — a parent preparing your things out of care.
아이 준비물 좀 챙겨줄래요?
Can you get the kid's supplies ready?
-ㄹ래요 makes a soft request to do the caring task on someone's behalf.
팀장님이 신입사원들을 하나하나 챙겨주셔서 다들 잘 적응했어요
Because the team lead looked after each new hire personally, everyone settled in well
Real-situation honorific 챙겨주시다 — here it means mentoring/taking care of people, not packing objects.
nuance: 챙겨주다 is 챙기다 (to gather up / see to what's needed) + 주다 (to give/do for), and it radiates warmth: you thoughtfully pull together someone's belongings, meals, or wellbeing because you care about them. The dividing line with the plain 주다 is the active 'seeing-to-it' nuance — 주다 merely transfers a thing, but 챙겨주다 implies you noticed what they'd need and took the trouble to prepare it, so Koreans use it about parents, partners, and caring seniors at work. It stretches figuratively too: 생일을 챙겨주다 (make a fuss of a birthday), 신입을 챙겨주다 (look out for a newcomer). The crucial pitfall: drop the 주 and 챙기다 alone means you do it for yourself (가방을 챙기다 = pack your own bag), so only 챙겨주다 expresses doing it for another. As a 주다 compound the forms are regular: 챙겨줘요, 챙겨줬어요, 챙겨주세요, and the honorific 챙겨주세요/챙겨주셨어요.

Don't confuse it with 챙기다's selfish reading 잇속을 챙기다 (look after one's own interests); adding 주다 flips the focus to the other person's benefit.

usage: The headword collocation — 짐/상자/물건을 나르다, repeatedly transporting things from one spot to another.
Classic moving-house scene; 나르다 implies many trips, not a single lift.
Shows 나르다 covers ferrying a substance repeatedly, e.g. buckets to a field.
Heavy, repetitive labor — the prototypical feel of 나르다 as effortful transport.
examples: 이 상자 좀 날라 줘
Carry this box over, please
반말 favor; 날라 줘 = 날라 (르 form) + 줘 asks a friend to haul it for you.
우리가 의자를 다 날랐어요
We carried all the chairs over
Past 날랐어요 shows the르 irregular doubling the ㄹ before 아.
이삿날 친구들이 와서 짐을 차까지 같이 날라 줬어요
On moving day my friends came and hauled the bags out to the car with me
Real-situation; 나르다 fits the repeated trips of carrying load after load.
nuance: 나르다 means to physically transport objects — usually heavy or numerous, like boxes, furniture, bricks, or water — from one place to another, typically over repeated trips, so it conveys effortful hauling rather than a single act. Contrast it with 들다 (to lift / hold in the hand): 들다 is just raising or holding something, while 나르다 is the whole job of relocating things across a distance, so you 들다 a single chair to look at it but 나르다 a roomful of chairs to a truck. Note also 옮기다, which simply means 'to move (something) to another place' and can be one item or one move; 나르다 specifically evokes the laborious, back-and-forth carrying. The key conjugation point is that 나르다 is a 르-irregular: before 아/어 the 르 splits and the previous syllable gains a ㄹ patchim, so 나르 + 아 → 날라, giving 날라요 and past 날랐어요. Before a consonant the stem is untouched: 나르고, 나르지, 나릅니다, and the future/potential keep it too — 나를 거예요, 나를 수 있어요.

usage: Standard restaurant/home request — fetch the thing and deliver it to me.
Figurative — an object or event 'brings' fortune; shows 가져다주다 isn't only literal fetching.
Abstract result use: something 가져다준다 a benefit or change to a person or situation.
to bring the parcel right to the door
Emphasizes delivery TO a destination/person, the heart of 가져다주다.
examples: 리모컨 좀 가져다줘
Bring me the remote
반말 everyday request; the listener fetches it and brings it back to you.
이 책 좀 동생에게 가져다줄래요?
Can you take this book to my younger sibling?
에게 marks the receiver; -ㄹ래요 softens it into a friendly ask.
주문하신 음료 자리로 가져다드리겠습니다
I'll bring your drink to your table
Real-situation service speech — to a customer it becomes the humble 가져다드리다.
nuance: 가져다주다 is built from 가지다 (to have/take) + the connective -다(가) + 주다 (to give), literally 'take it and then give it', i.e. go fetch something and bring it to a person. The sharp contrast to learn is direction: 가져다주다 brings the item TOWARD the receiver, whereas 가져가다 (take + go) carries it AWAY from here, and 가져오다 (take + come) just means bring it here without the 'for someone' nuance — so a server 가져다준다 your water (brings and hands it to you), but a customer 가져간다 the leftovers (takes them away). It also works abstractly: 행운을/변화를 가져다주다 'to bring luck/change'. When serving someone of higher status, raise the verb to 가져다드리다 (가져다드리겠습니다). As a 주다 compound all forms are regular and predictable: 가져다줘요, 가져다줬어요, 가져다주세요, honorific 가져다주세요/가져다주셨어요.

Don't keep plain 주다 when serving an elder or customer — politely it becomes 가져다드릴게요 / 가져다드리겠습니다.

english: to carry on one's shoulder / back
usage: to carry a bag (over the shoulder)
The defining collocation — 가방/배낭/책가방을 메다, anything worn by a strap on shoulder or back.
to go with a backpack on
메고 + motion verb describes doing something while wearing the bag.
to sling a rifle (over the shoulder)
Shows 메다 covers strapped/slung items generally, not just school bags.
어깨에 spells out the body part; reinforces that 메다 is shoulder/back-borne carrying.
examples: 가방 메고 와
Come with your bag on
반말; 메고 오다 tells someone to arrive wearing the bag.
무거운 배낭을 멨어요
I carried a heavy backpack
Past 멨어요 — the ㅔ stem contracts 메 + 었 down to 멨.
등산 갈 때는 양쪽 어깨로 배낭을 메야 허리가 안 아파요
When hiking you should carry the backpack on both shoulders so your back doesn't hurt
Real-situation advice; 메야 (메 + 어야) shows the obligation form of a ㅔ-stem verb.
nuance: 메다 means to carry something by slinging it on your shoulder or back with a strap — a backpack, a satchel, even a rifle. The dividing line you must keep clear is with 들다 (to carry in the hand): a handbag held in your fist is 들다, but the moment a strap goes over your shoulder it becomes 메다, so 가방을 들다 and 가방을 메다 picture two different postures. Also beware the homophone-ish 매다 'to tie/fasten' (넥타이를 매다, 신발끈을 매다) — same romanization, different spelling and meaning, and mixing them up is the number-one native-and-learner trip-up here. Conjugation is straightforward because the stem ends in the vowel ㅔ: 메 + 어 contracts to plain 메, so the 요-form is 메요, the past is 멨어요, and the obligation form is 메야 해요 (never 메어요 / 메었어요).

Don't write the past as 메었어요 — the ㅔ stem contracts, so it is 멨어요.

usage: to carry a baby on one's back
The prototypical collocation — 업다 almost always pictures a baby or small child piggybacked.
to be carrying (someone) on one's back
업고 있다 describes the ongoing state of holding someone piggyback right now.
등에 names the back explicitly; reinforces the body location of the action.
to raise (a child) on one's back
Idiomatic warmth — to have lovingly raised a child, evoked by the piggyback image.
examples: 아기 업어 줄까?
Shall I carry the baby on my back?
반말 offer; 업어 줘 = 업어 + 주- offers to piggyback for someone.
엄마가 아이를 업었어요
Mom carried the child on her back
Past 업었어요 — note the ㅂ stays, since 업다 is a regular verb, not ㅂ-irregular.
다친 친구를 업고 한참을 걸어서 병원까지 갔어요
I carried my injured friend on my back and walked a long way to the hospital
Real-situation; 업고 가다 (piggyback + go) for helping someone who can't walk.
nuance: 업다 means to carry a person — almost always a baby, small child, or someone who can't walk — on your back, piggyback style, and it carries a tender, caregiving warmth (hence 업어 키우다 'to raise lovingly'). Distinguish it from 안다 'to hold in your arms / hug against your chest': a fussy infant facing you is 안다, but settled against your back it is 업다, two different holds. The pitfall that trips nearly every learner is the conjugation: 업다 looks like it should be a ㅂ-irregular (turning ㅂ into 우), but it is a perfectly regular consonant-stem verb, so the ㅂ stays put — 업 + 어 → 업어요, past 업었어요, potential 업을 수 있어요, polite command 업으세요. Saying 어워요 is wrong. Finally keep it apart from the look-alike 엎다 'to overturn / knock over' (그릇을 엎다), which is spelled with ㅍ and means something completely different.

Don't use 안다 when the person is on your back — 안다 is holding in your arms against the chest; the back-carry is 업다.
Don't spell it 엎다 — that ㅍ verb means to overturn/tip over (그릇을 엎다), nothing to do with carrying a person.

usage: to load luggage into the car
The core frame — 물건/짐/화물을 (vehicle)에 싣다, putting cargo onto a means of transport.
Vehicle marked with 에; 싣다 specifically targets cars, trucks, ships, trains.
to carry (a story) in an article
Figurative — a newspaper '싣는다' a piece, i.e. publishes/runs it; a common extended sense.
to sing putting one's heart into it
Abstract — to 'load' feeling onto something; shows 싣다 can carry emotion or meaning.
examples: 이거 차에 실어 줘
Load this into the car for me
반말 favor; 실어 줘 = 실어 (ㄷ→ㄹ form) + 줘 asks someone to load it for you.
상자를 트럭에 실었어요
I loaded the boxes onto the truck
Past 실었어요 — before the vowel the ㄷ has turned to ㄹ (ㄷ irregular).
짐이 너무 많아서 한 번에 다 실을 수 없었어요
There was so much luggage we couldn't load it all at once
Real-situation; potential 실을 수 from the ㄷ-irregular stem before -ㄹ 수.
nuance: 싣다 means to load cargo, luggage, or goods ONTO a vehicle — a car, truck, ship, train, or plane — and it implies placing things on/in a means of transport, marked by 에 (트럭에 싣다). Contrast it with 담다 'to put into a container' (그릇에 담다, 가방에 담다): you 담다 rice into a bowl but you 싣다 boxes onto a truck, because 싣다 specifically targets transport, not ordinary containers. It also extends figuratively — 기사를 싣다 'to run an article', 마음을 실어 'putting one's heart into it'. The make-or-break point is that 싣다 is a ㄷ-irregular verb: before a vowel ending the final ㄷ changes to ㄹ, so 싣 + 어 → 실어요, past 실었어요, potential 실을 수 있어요, command 실으세요. Before a consonant the ㄷ is kept intact: 싣고, 싣지, 싣습니다. Mixing these two stems up is the classic error.

Don't use 담다 for putting things onto a vehicle — 담다 is filling a container/bowl/bag, while loading onto a truck or car is 싣다.

usage: The headword pattern — 간식/사탕/프린트를 나눠주다, giving one portion each to many people.
Classroom/meeting staple; 나눠주다 = pass a copy to everyone present.
to share the food out evenly
골고루 'evenly' pairs naturally, since 나눠주다 implies dividing among several.
to dole out allowance / pocket money
Distributing money in portions to multiple recipients (e.g. to several kids).
examples: 사탕 좀 나눠줘
Share out some candy
반말; 나눠줘 asks a friend to dole pieces out to the group.
선생님이 학생들에게 프린트를 나눠줬어요
The teacher handed printouts to the students
에게 marks the recipients; the classic distribute-to-a-class scene.
봉사자들이 길에서 따뜻한 국밥을 한 그릇씩 나눠줬어요
The volunteers handed out a bowl of warm soup each on the street
Real-situation; 씩 'each' underlines the one-portion-per-person sense of 나눠주다.
nuance: 나눠주다 is 나누다 (to divide / share / split) + 주다 (to give), so it means to break something into portions and hand one to each of several people — passing out snacks, handouts, or money to a group. The key contrast is with bare 나누다, which by itself only means 'to divide' or 'to share/have in common' (나누다 can also mean 대화를 나누다 'to share a conversation'); it lacks the explicit 'give it out to people' direction that the +주다 supplies, so 사탕을 나누다 sounds incomplete where 사탕을 나눠주다 is the natural 'hand the candy out'. Compare too 돌리다 (to pass/hand around, e.g. 떡을 돌리다 'distribute rice cakes to neighbors'), which overlaps but stresses circulating among a circle. The implied plurality of recipients is what separates 나눠주다 from one-to-one 건네다/주다. As a 주다 compound the conjugation is fully regular: 나눠줘요, 나눠줬어요, 나눠주세요.

usage: The core collocation — extend a hand for a shake, for help, or to receive something.
내밀다 also covers thrusting a body part forward/out, e.g. peeking out a window.
Everyday gesture; shows the 'push it forward/out' core of 내밀다.
to reach out a helping hand
Set figurative phrase — to offer help; the extended-hand image stands for assistance.
examples: 손 내밀어 봐
Hold out your hand
반말; 내밀어 봐 = 내밀- + 어 봐 'try holding it out' — the ㄹ stays before the vowel 어.
창밖으로 손을 내밀지 마세요
Don't stick your hand out the window
Polite negative command; -지 마세요 keeps the full stem 내밀-.
그가 첫인사로 손을 내밀며 악수를 청했어요
He held out his hand as a first greeting and asked for a handshake
Real-situation; 내밀며 (내밀- + -며) describes presenting something toward someone.
nuance: 내밀다 is 내- (out) + 밀다 (to push), literally 'to push outward', and it means to thrust or extend something forward — a hand, your head, your tongue, or an object you're presenting like a ticket or business card. The contrast to draw is with 내놓다 'to put out / set out' (음식을 내놓다, 의견을 내놓다): 내놓다 places or releases something out into the open, while 내밀다 specifically pushes it forward toward a person or through an opening, so you 손을 내밀다 (thrust your hand out to someone) but 쓰레기를 내놓다 (set the trash out). It carries a warm idiom, 도움의 손길을 내밀다 'to reach out a helping hand'. The conjugation pitfall is that 내밀다 is a ㄹ-stem verb where the ㄹ drops before ㅂ, ㄴ, and ㅅ: hence formal 내밉니다 (not 내밀습니다) and polite command 내미세요 (not 내밀으세요). Before a vowel the ㄹ stays: 내밀어요, 내밀었어요.

usage: Please pass this to my friend
The core favor pattern — relay an object or note to a third person on the speaker's behalf.
Extremely common set phrase; 안부 'greetings/news of one's wellbeing' is the classic thing relayed.
Figurative — to communicate heartfelt feelings to someone, often via a gift or message.
말씀 is the humble/honorific word for 'words/message'; used when the message is for/from someone respected.
examples: 엄마한테 이거 전해줘
Pass this to mom for me
반말; 전해줘 asks a family member to deliver it to a third person.
이 편지를 선생님께 전해줬어요
I delivered this letter to the teacher
께 is the honorific of 에게, raising the recipient (the teacher) you handed it to.
회의 결과를 사장님께 잘 전해드리겠습니다
I'll be sure to relay the meeting results to the CEO
Real-situation honorific — to a superior, 전해주다 becomes the humble 전해드리다.
nuance: 전해주다 is 전하다 (傳하다, 傳 'to transmit/convey') + 주다 (to give), so the Sino-Korean root literally means 'to pass something along and give it', i.e. to deliver an object, message, or feeling to someone — very often through a third person. It handles both physical things (a letter, a gift) and intangibles (안부를 전해줘요 'send my regards', 마음을 전해주다 'convey one's feelings'). The dividing line with 보내다 'to send' is distance and channel: 보내다 dispatches something across a gap (편지를 보내다 'mail a letter', 문자를 보내다 'send a text'), while 전해주다 emphasizes the item actually reaching and being handed to the recipient, frequently in person or via a go-between. To a superior, raise 주다 to the humble 드리다 → 전해드리다 (전해드리겠습니다), and use 께 for the honored recipient. As a 주다 compound the forms are regular: 전해줘요, 전해줬어요, 전해주세요.
